title: TLS and HTTPS handshake cost
scopeHtml: Scope: what TLS guarantees, symmetric vs asymmetric crypto, certificates and chains, the TLS 1.3 handshake, resumption and 0-RTT, termination choices, handshake cost reduction and pinning.

notes.title: What TLS gives you
notes.html:
TLS (Transport Layer Security) wraps a connection so nobody in the middle can read it, change it, or pretend to be the server. HTTPS is just HTTP carried over TLS. Three promises:

  1. Confidentiality: data is encrypted; Wi-Fi owners and ISPs see only that you talk to an IP.
  2. Integrity: any tampering is detected (each record has an authentication tag).
  3. Authentication: the server proves it is really shop.com using a certificate signed by a trusted authority. Optionally the client proves itself too (mutual TLS).

Worked example. On public coffee-shop Wi-Fi, over plain HTTP anyone can read your cookie and replay it. Over HTTPS the same bytes are ciphertext; an attacker sees only the destination IP and (via SNI, unless ECH) the hostname.

Industry examples. Browsers mark HTTP pages "Not secure"; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are used over TLS in practice; Google, Cloudflare and Let's Encrypt pushed HTTPS from about 30% to over 90% of web traffic. Android blocks cleartext traffic by default from API 28 (usesCleartextTraffic), relevant for app developers.

Everyday analogy. A sealed, tamper-evident envelope delivered by a courier who first checks the receiver's government ID.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying HTTPS makes the server secure. It protects data in transit only.
  • Thinking encryption alone is enough; without authentication you may be encrypting to an attacker (man in the middle).
  • Forgetting that the destination host is still partly visible to the network.

notes.title: Symmetric, asymmetric and the key idea of the handshake
notes.html:
Asymmetric crypto is slow but lets strangers agree on a secret; symmetric crypto is fast but needs a shared secret. TLS uses both: asymmetric (key exchange and signatures) to set up, then symmetric for all bulk data.

  • Symmetric (AES-128/256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305): one key encrypts and decrypts; runs at multiple GB/s with hardware support (AES-NI). ChaCha20 is faster on phones without AES hardware.
  • Asymmetric: a key pair. Signatures (RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519) prove identity. Key exchange (ECDHE, X25519) lets both sides compute the same secret over an open wire without ever sending it. Ephemeral (the E in ECDHE) keys give forward secrecy: if the server's long-term key leaks later, old recordings still cannot be decrypted.

Worked example. Handshake cost on a server: an ECDSA P-256 signature takes about 0.05 ms, an RSA-2048 signature about 1 ms (about 20x slower), so a 16-core box does maybe 15k RSA handshakes/s versus hundreds of thousands of ECDSA. Bulk data after that costs almost nothing: AES-GCM with hardware does several GB/s per core.

Industry examples. Let's Encrypt issues ECDSA certificates; Cloudflare serves both ECDSA and RSA depending on client. Signal and WhatsApp apply the same idea (key exchange then symmetric ciphers) for end-to-end messaging, a different layer from TLS.

Decision gravity. Choice of certificate key type (ECDSA vs RSA) is reversible by reissuing; very old clients (Android 4, Windows XP) may need RSA. Forward secrecy should be non-negotiable.

Everyday analogy. Two people shout paint colours across a crowded room and each mixes with a private colour; both end up with the same final shade the crowd cannot work out. Then they use that shade as the password for a fast lock.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "data is encrypted with the public key". Bulk data uses a symmetric session key.
  • Confusing encryption with signing.
  • Not knowing what forward secrecy means.

notes.title: Certificates and the chain of trust
notes.html:
A certificate is a signed statement: "this public key belongs to shop.com", signed by a Certificate Authority (CA) your device already trusts. Servers usually send a chain: leaf certificate (shop.com), an intermediate CA certificate, and the client has the root in its trust store (OS or browser, roughly 100+ roots).

The client checks: signature chain to a trusted root, hostname matches the certificate's Subject Alternative Name (SAN), validity dates (now commonly 90 days for Let's Encrypt; the industry is heading to shorter lifetimes, confirm current CA/Browser Forum limits), and revocation status (CRL, OCSP, and OCSP stapling where the server attaches a fresh signed response to avoid an extra lookup).

Config example (nginx).

# Let's Encrypt via certbot, auto-renew
certbot certonly --nginx -d shop.com -d www.shop.com
# nginx
#   ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/shop.com/fullchain.pem;
#   ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/shop.com/privkey.pem;
#   ssl_stapling on; ssl_stapling_verify on;

fullchain.pem must include the intermediate; a missing intermediate works in some browsers (they fetch it) and fails in Android/curl/Java clients.

Production incident pattern. Expired certificate: at midnight every request fails with CERTIFICATE_EXPIRED/handshake failure; error rate goes to 100% while servers look healthy. Famous cases: many companies, including large cloud and telecom providers, have had outages from an expired cert or expired intermediate. Fix: automate renewal (ACME), alert at 30, 14, 7 days, monitor expiry from outside.

Industry examples. Let's Encrypt (free, automated, ACME), AWS ACM (free certs on ALB/CloudFront, auto-renew, but cannot export private key), DigiCert. Google, Mozilla and Apple enforce Certificate Transparency logs.

Decision gravity. Where certificate private keys live (HSM, KMS, load balancer) is hard to change later. Wildcard certs are convenient but a leak exposes every subdomain.

Everyday analogy. A passport: you trust it because a government you recognise issued it, it has not expired, and the name matches the person standing in front of you.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the intermediate certificate.
  • No expiry monitoring.
  • Disabling certificate verification "just for testing" and shipping it (a top mobile security finding).

notes.title: The TLS 1.3 handshake step by step
notes.html:
TLS 1.3 needs one round trip to set up a new connection. (TLS 1.2 needed two.)

  1. ClientHello: supported ciphers, a fresh random, a key share (client's ECDHE public value, guessed for X25519), SNI (hostname), ALPN (h2/h3).
  2. ServerHello + encrypted rest: server's key share; both now derive keys. The server then sends, already encrypted: its certificate, a signature over the handshake (CertificateVerify) and Finished.
  3. Client Finished. Client can send the HTTP request right in this flight.
Client                                   Server
 | -- ClientHello (key share, SNI) ----> |
 | <- ServerHello (key share)            |   1 RTT
 |    {Certificate, Verify, Finished} -- |
 | -- {Finished} + HTTP request -------> |
 | <---------- HTTP response ----------- |

Worked example. Over TCP, RTT 50 ms: TCP handshake 50 ms + TLS 1.3 50 ms = 100 ms, request at 100 ms, response at 150 ms plus server time. With TLS 1.2: 50 + 100 = 150 ms before the request. Over QUIC the transport and TLS combine: 50 ms.

Industry examples. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) is enabled by default in Chrome, Android 10+, iOS 12.2+ and by Cloudflare, AWS ALB and nginx. It removed weak options (RC4, static RSA key exchange, CBC modes, compression) for safety.

Decision gravity. Enable TLS 1.3 and keep 1.2 as the floor; disabling 1.2 can strand old clients. Disabling 1.0/1.1 is standard (PCI requires it). All reversible config.

Everyday analogy. Exchanging a secret handshake in one quick move: "here's my half of the secret and what I can do", "here's mine plus my ID", done.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting the TLS 1.2 two-RTT cost for 1.3.
  • Forgetting the TCP handshake RTT that precedes TLS.
  • Thinking the certificate is used to encrypt data. It authenticates the key exchange.

notes.title: Session resumption and 0-RTT
notes.html:
After the first handshake, a client and server can skip the expensive parts next time. The server gives the client a session ticket (encrypted state the server can later decrypt, so no per-session server storage with ticket keys shared across servers). On reconnect the client sends the ticket (a pre-shared key, PSK) and, in TLS 1.3, may skip the certificate and signature: fewer CPU cycles and smaller handshake. Resumption still takes 1 RTT.

0-RTT (early data) goes further: the client sends the HTTP request in the first flight using the PSK, with zero extra round trip. The catch: early data is replayable. An attacker can capture and resend that first packet, and the server may process it twice. So servers should only accept 0-RTT for idempotent requests (GET), and many disable it for POST. Cloudflare adds a Early-Data: 1 header so origins can reject with 425 Too Early.

Worked example. A mobile app reconnecting after backgrounding with RTT 120 ms: full handshake over TCP+TLS1.3 = 240 ms before the request; with TLS resumption it is still 240 ms but cheaper CPU on the server; with QUIC 0-RTT it is 0 ms setup. Server CPU: resumed handshakes skip the signature, so a box that did 15k full handshakes/s may do several times more resumed ones.

Ticket key management. In a fleet, all servers must share ticket-encryption keys, rotated often (for example every 12 to 24 hours, keeping the previous key for decrypt). A leaked ticket key weakens forward secrecy for sessions that used tickets, so rotate and do not persist it to disk.

Industry examples. Cloudflare and Google rotate ticket keys regularly across the global fleet. Chrome and Safari use 0-RTT for GET over HTTP/3.

Decision gravity. Enabling 0-RTT trades a bit of latency for replay risk; an easily reversible setting but a security review item. Default to off for state-changing endpoints.

Everyday analogy. A gym membership card: the first visit needs ID and paperwork, later visits you flash the card and walk in. But a stolen card can be reused, so you only let it open the cafe, not the vault.

Common interview traps.

  • Allowing 0-RTT on payment POSTs.
  • Per-server ticket keys, so resumption fails after a load balancer picks a different server.
  • Confusing session IDs (server state) and session tickets (client-held state).

notes.title: Where TLS terminates and what it costs
notes.html:
TLS termination means the place where encryption stops and plain HTTP (or re-encrypted traffic) begins. Choices:

Option How Pros Cons
Terminate at the LB / CDN Client TLS ends at edge; LB talks HTTP to servers Centralised certs, offloaded CPU, L7 features Plain traffic inside the network
Re-encrypt (TLS to backend) Edge terminates then opens new TLS to server Encrypted everywhere Double CPU, certs on servers
Passthrough (L4) LB forwards encrypted bytes untouched End-to-end, LB cannot read No L7 routing, no WAF
mTLS in service mesh Sidecars (Envoy/Istio) encrypt service to service with identities Zero-trust, auto-rotated certs Operational complexity, latency ~1 ms

Cost numbers. Modern CPUs with AES-NI: TLS adds under 1 to 2% CPU for bulk traffic (Google reported TLS is not a computational burden). The expensive part is handshakes (asymmetric): about 0.1 to 1 ms CPU per full handshake. Memory about 10 to 50 KB per connection. The big real cost is latency of handshakes on cold connections, not throughput.

Config example (nginx modern profile).

# nginx.conf essentials
# ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
# ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:50m;     # ~200k sessions per 50 MB
# ssl_session_timeout 1d;
# ssl_session_tickets on;
# ssl_stapling on;
# add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;

Industry examples. Netflix and Google use mTLS between internal services (ALTS at Google). AWS ALB terminates TLS with ACM certs; many regulated companies (payments) re-encrypt to meet PCI scope. Amazon CloudFront terminates close to the user so the long-haul leg to origin reuses warm connections.

Decision gravity. Terminate at the edge is cheap and reversible. Adopting a mesh with mTLS is a platform commitment that is expensive to undo but valuable for zero trust.

Everyday analogy. Security at an airport: either check passengers once at the main gate and trust the inside, or check them again at every door of every building.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying TLS is too slow to use everywhere. Handshakes are the cost, not encryption.
  • Forgetting that terminating at the LB means plain traffic in the VPC, a compliance question.
  • Not mentioning HSTS (forces HTTPS and prevents downgrade).

notes.title: Handshake cost in a real design and mobile pinning
notes.html:
Where handshake cost bites: cold mobile clients, serverless/short-lived processes, service calls without pooling, and global users far from the origin.

Ways to cut it:

  1. Terminate near the user (CDN or regional edge) so the handshake RTT is short, e.g. 10 ms instead of 200 ms.
  2. Reuse connections (keep-alive, HTTP/2, pooled clients with sensible idle timeouts).
  3. TLS 1.3, ECDSA certs, OCSP stapling, small cert chain (fewer bytes; a chain over about 14 KB spills past the initial TCP window and costs an extra RTT).
  4. Resumption / 0-RTT for idempotent calls.
  5. HTTP/3 to merge handshakes.
  6. Preconnect hints in web pages (<link rel="preconnect">).

Worked example. User in Sydney, origin in Virginia (RTT 200 ms): direct, TCP+TLS1.3 = 400 ms before request. Through a CDN with an edge 10 ms away: user-to-edge handshakes = 20 ms, and the edge keeps a warm connection to origin, so total first byte is about 20 ms + 200 ms for a cache miss, or just 20 ms on a hit.

Certificate pinning (mobile). An app can pin the expected public key or certificate so even a rogue CA cannot impersonate your server. Gravity: it is risky; if you rotate keys without updating the app, old versions stop working. Safer: pin to the SPKI hash of an intermediate or keep backup pins (Android's network_security_config supports <pin-set> with expiry). Many teams now rely on certificate transparency and avoid hard pinning.

Production incident pattern. After a deploy or cert rotation, SSLHandshakeException spikes on older Android clients: missing intermediate or removed old root (the Let's Encrypt ISRG Root X1 / DST Root CA X3 expiry in 2021 broke old devices). Metric: handshake failure rate by client version.

Everyday analogy. Opening a bank branch near every customer so the ID check happens round the corner, and the branch keeps a direct private line to head office.

Common interview traps.

  • Hard-pinning a leaf certificate with no backup.
  • Ignoring chain size and old-device root compatibility.
  • Not separating "first request" latency from steady state.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• TLS gives confidentiality, integrity and authentication; HTTPS = HTTP over TLS. It protects data in transit only.
  • Asymmetric crypto (ECDHE key exchange, signatures) sets up; symmetric (AES-GCM, ChaCha20) carries data. Ephemeral keys give forward secrecy.
  • Certificates form a chain to a trusted root; check hostname, expiry, revocation (OCSP stapling). Automate renewal and alert on expiry: expired certs cause total outages.
  • TLS 1.3 handshake is 1 RTT (1.2 was 2); add the TCP handshake RTT for total setup; QUIC merges them.
  • Resumption tickets cut CPU; 0-RTT removes a round trip but is replayable, so allow it only for idempotent requests; share and rotate ticket keys across the fleet.
  • Terminate TLS at the edge or LB for simplicity, re-encrypt or use mTLS inside for compliance and zero trust; bulk encryption is cheap, handshakes on cold connections are the cost.
  • Reduce cost with edge termination, connection reuse, TLS 1.3, ECDSA, small chains and HTTP/3; be careful with certificate pinning.

questions.promptHtml: What does HTTPS actually protect, and what does it not protect?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates say "HTTPS makes it secure". The signal is whether you can name the three guarantees and the limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: HTTPS is HTTP carried inside TLS. TLS gives me three things: confidentiality (nobody on the path can read the bytes), integrity (any change is detected) and authentication (the server proves it owns the hostname through a certificate). It protects data in transit only. It does not make the server code safe, it does not hide the destination IP, and the hostname is usually visible through SNI unless ECH is used.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without TLS, anyone on the Wi-Fi or any hop can read cookies and replay them. With TLS the same bytes are ciphertext with an authentication tag on every record, so a flipped bit makes decryption fail instead of silently changing a payment amount.

Authentication matters as much as encryption. If you encrypt to an attacker (man in the middle) you have confidentiality against everyone except the one person who matters. The certificate chain is what ties the key to the name shop.com.

Visible to the network      Hidden from the network
-------------------------   -------------------------
destination IP, port        URL path, query string
SNI hostname (no ECH)       headers, cookies, body
traffic size and timing     response content

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying HTTPS secures the server. SQL injection over HTTPS is still SQL injection.
  • Thinking encryption without authentication is enough.
  • Forgetting that the endpoint after the load balancer may be plain HTTP.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who can still see which sites I visit on HTTPS? -> The ISP sees IPs and usually the SNI hostname; not the path or content.
  2. What is mutual TLS? -> The client also presents a certificate, so the server authenticates the client; common between services.
  3. Does HTTPS stop replay or CSRF? -> No. TLS protects the channel, not application-level request semantics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it encrypts data". The senior names integrity and authentication, states the in-transit scope, and mentions what metadata leaks and where TLS ends in the architecture.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that terminate TLS at the load balancer and run plain HTTP inside the VPC have failed compliance reviews because "HTTPS everywhere" did not cover the internal hop.

questions.subtopic: Symmetric vs asymmetric and forward secrecy
questions.promptHtml: Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography, and what is forward secrecy?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks that you understand the handshake as "set up a shared secret, then use a fast cipher", not "encrypt with the public key".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Asymmetric crypto is slow but lets two strangers agree on a secret and prove identity with signatures. Symmetric crypto like AES-GCM is fast but needs a shared key. So TLS uses ECDHE key exchange plus a signature to agree on a session key, then encrypts all data with AES or ChaCha20. Forward secrecy means the key exchange uses throwaway (ephemeral) keys, so if the server's long-term key leaks later, recorded old traffic still cannot be decrypted.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cost matters. An ECDSA P-256 signature is about 0.05 ms, RSA-2048 about 1 ms (about 20x slower). AES-GCM with AES-NI moves several GB/s per core. So the asymmetric work is paid once per connection and the bulk data is almost free.

1. Client and server each make a fresh ECDHE key pair (ephemeral)
2. They swap public halves; both compute the same shared secret
3. Server signs the handshake transcript with its certificate key
   (proves identity; this key is NOT used to encrypt data)
4. Both derive session keys -> AES-GCM / ChaCha20 for all records
5. Ephemeral private keys are deleted -> forward secrecy

ChaCha20-Poly1305 is preferred on phones without AES hardware.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "The data is encrypted with the server's public key." Bulk data uses the symmetric session key.
  • Confusing encryption (confidentiality) with signing (authenticity).
  • Static RSA key exchange has no forward secrecy; TLS 1.3 removed it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a leaked server private key less harmful with ECDHE? -> Past session keys came from deleted ephemeral values, not from that key.
  2. ECDSA or RSA certificates? -> ECDSA for CPU and size; RSA only for very old clients.
  3. Where does forward secrecy weaken? -> Session tickets: a leaked ticket key can decrypt resumed sessions, so rotate it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer repeats "asymmetric is slow, symmetric is fast". The senior adds the signature-versus-key-exchange split, the numbers, forward secrecy and the ticket-key caveat.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A key leak from a compromised backup was far less damaging for a team that had ECDHE-only suites, because stored packet captures stayed unreadable.

questions.contextHtml:
Your team renewed the certificate for api.shop.com on the load balancer at 10:00. Chrome and Safari work. Within minutes the support channel reports that the Android app and a partner's Java service fail. Error rate from Android is 100%, web is 0%. The new cert came from the same CA and has 60 days left. Logs:

okhttp: javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException:
  Trust anchor for certification path not found.
curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate

Someone suggests it is a CDN problem. Someone else suggests turning off verification in the app config as a hotfix.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you confirm it, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the CDN or the Android release, proposes disabling certificate verification, or just "renews again". It misses that browsers can fetch a missing intermediate on their own while other clients cannot.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did we change the bundle file at renewal (cert only vs fullchain)? Which clients fail (all non-browser)? Did the web and app hit the same endpoint? Any change in CA or root?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reinstall the certificate with the full chain (leaf plus intermediate) on the load balancer. Do not touch client verification; a hotfix that disables checks is a security incident.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) intermediate missing from what the server sends, (b) CA moved to a new intermediate not in older trust stores, (c) wrong chain order, (d) CDN serving an old cert on some POPs.
  4. How I'd verify each: openssl s_client -connect api.shop.com:443 -servername api.shop.com -showcerts and count the certs sent; a chain of depth 1 plus "verify error: unable to get local issuer certificate" confirms (a). Compare against curl -v from a clean container. Check each CDN POP with --resolve.
  5. Root cause: The server sent only the leaf. Browsers use AIA (authority information access) to download the missing intermediate and cache it, so they work. Android, Java and curl do not, so they cannot build a path to a trusted root.
  6. Fix: Short term: deploy fullchain.pem. Long term: a post-deploy synthetic check that connects with a strict client (openssl with no cached certs) and fails the pipeline if verification fails.
  7. Prevention: Test with a client that does not fetch intermediates; alert on handshake failure rate by client type; a runbook that says "always fullchain".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not disable verification or pin around the problem. I would not blame the CDN before looking at the chain the server actually sends.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Chain order is wrong, does it matter? -> Some clients tolerate it, strict ones fail; send leaf first, then intermediates.
  • Should the root be included in the chain? -> No, clients already have it; it only wastes bytes.
  • Only old Android 7 devices fail after a CA change. -> Their trust store lacks the new root; use a cross-signed chain or an alternate chain from the CA.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team renewed on a Friday evening, tested in the browser only and shipped. The mobile app and a payments webhook partner broke overnight. The fix was a one-line file path change, but the lesson was adding a strict-client check to the deploy.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests disabling verification or blames the client app.
  • Hire: identifies missing intermediate and uses openssl s_client to prove it.
  • Strong hire: also explains why browsers mask it, adds a strict-client deploy gate and a failure-rate-by-client alert.

questions.contextHtml: Your product manager says: "Users in Sydney complain the first load of the app feels slow, about 1 second before anything appears. Make the TLS faster." Your origin is in Virginia. Measured RTT Sydney to Virginia is 200 ms. The load balancer currently allows TLS 1.2 and 1.3. The server time for the first API call is 40 ms. The browser shows connect 200 ms, SSL 200 ms, wait 440 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Where does the time go and what would you change, in order?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to a faster cipher" or "get a bigger server". The cipher is not the cost; round trips over a long-haul path are.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which client versions negotiate TLS 1.3 (the SSL 200 ms suggests 1.3 already; 1.2 would show 400 ms)? Is the 440 ms wait mostly network? Is the response cacheable? Can we add a CDN?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I start with the math. TCP handshake 200 ms, TLS 1.3 handshake 200 ms, request and response 200 ms plus 40 ms server = 640 ms of network plus server before the first byte plus the 440 wait seen above. TLS 1.2 would be 200 + 400 = 600 ms before the request.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the cost is distance (RTT x 3 round trips), not crypto. Crypto adds under 1 ms of CPU.
  4. How I'd verify: browser timing breakdown or curl -w "connect:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer}\n" from a Sydney host; openssl s_client -tls1_3 to confirm version.
  5. Root cause: Long RTT times a fixed number of round trips.
  6. Fix: (1) Terminate TLS at a CDN edge about 10 ms away: user handshakes cost about 20 ms each; the edge keeps a warm TLS connection to Virginia. (2) Enable HTTP/3 so transport and TLS handshakes merge to one RTT. (3) Reuse connections and resumption for repeat visits. (4) Cache the HTML shell at the edge so a hit costs about 20 ms. (5) Preconnect hint for the API host.
  7. Prevention: Track TTFB by region as an SLO.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not tune cipher suites for latency. A CDN adds cost and a cache-key design job, but it is reversible. I would not enable 0-RTT for POSTs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Everything is dynamic and uncacheable. -> The edge still saves the two handshakes; first byte drops from about 640 ms to about 20 + 200 + 40 = 260 ms.
  • Why not just open a second region? -> Data and write routing make it a one-way door; do the CDN first.
  • Does a smaller certificate help? -> A chain over about 14 KB can add a round trip in the initial TCP window; use ECDSA and a short chain.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team spent a sprint benchmarking AES variants for a "slow TLS" complaint. A CDN in front of the same origin cut Sydney first load from 1.1 s to 0.3 s with a DNS change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: talks about cipher speed.
  • Hire: counts round trips and moves termination to the edge.
  • Strong hire: quantifies each option, separates first visit from steady state, mentions HTTP/3, chain size and measurement.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments team enabled 0-RTT on their nginx edge to shave 100 ms from mobile checkout. Two weeks later reconciliation finds 31 duplicate charges out of 4 million orders, all on flaky mobile networks. Config:

# nginx.conf (excerpt, shown as YAML-ish key/value for readability)
ssl_protocols: TLSv1.3
ssl_early_data: "on"
location /v1/payments:
  proxy_pass: http://payments_pool
  # no Early-Data header forwarded

The payments service has no idempotency keys. The load balancer retries once on connection reset.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, and how do you fix it without giving up the latency win everywhere?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Network glitch, add retries" or "turn off TLS 1.3". It misses that early data is replayable and that the app cannot tell.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which endpoints get early data? Does the backend know a request came as early data? Do clients send idempotency keys? Are the duplicates identical request bodies?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable ssl_early_data for /v1/payments now, or reply 425 Too Early to any early-data POST.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 0-RTT replay of POST, (b) client retry after timeout, (c) LB retry on reset, (d) double submit from the app UI.
  4. How I'd verify each: log $ssl_early_data per request; correlate duplicates with value 1. Compare duplicate timestamps (replays are near-identical and may arrive on a different connection). Check LB retry settings.
  5. Root cause: 0-RTT data is encrypted with the PSK from an earlier session, so an attacker or a flaky network can resend the first flight. The server cannot distinguish a replay from a first send. Without a forwarded header and without idempotency, the app executes twice.
  6. Fix: Short term: forward proxy_set_header Early-Data $ssl_early_data; and return 425 for non-GET when it is 1. Long term: mandatory idempotency keys on payments, enforced server side (unique key, store result).
  7. Prevention: Allow 0-RTT only for GET and other safe methods; add a test that replays a captured early-data POST; code review rule for state-changing endpoints.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not keep 0-RTT on for money paths for 100 ms. Keeping it for GET static and catalogue calls is fine. I would not rely on "replays are rare".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does a client retry on 425 safely? -> Yes, browsers retry the request after the handshake completes, so it is no longer early data.
  • Could replay happen with normal 1-RTT TLS? -> No; the handshake randoms make normal data non-replayable. The app-level retry is a separate issue idempotency keys solve.
  • What about HTTP/3? -> Same 0-RTT replay property applies.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A checkout team celebrated a 12% faster first request, then found double-created orders only for users on trains. The cause was early data replay across a carrier proxy. Idempotency keys fixed it for good.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames retries only.
  • Hire: identifies replayable early data and disables it for POST.
  • Strong hire: forwards Early-Data, uses 425, adds idempotency keys and a replay test.

questions.contextHtml: You run an e-commerce API at 8,000 requests/s behind an AWS ALB that terminates TLS using ACM certificates; traffic to the pods is plain HTTP inside the VPC. A new payments compliance review says "card data must be encrypted in transit on every hop". Engineering has three options: keep it, re-encrypt to the pods, or switch to an L4 passthrough NLB with TLS on the pods. The platform team prefers the service mesh with mTLS. You have 6 weeks.
questions.promptHtml: Which option do you pick and how do you decide?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "TLS is slow, so keep plain HTTP" or "encrypt everything everywhere" with no cost, ops or decision-gravity thinking.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the review scope cover all services or only those handling card data? Is the WAF or L7 routing needed at the edge? Who owns certificate lifecycle for pods? Is there a mesh already?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. First confirm scope: only the payments path may need it, which cuts work.
  3. Hypotheses (options) ranked: (a) ALB terminates, re-encrypt to pods with TLS (keeps WAF and routing, needs certs on pods); (b) mesh mTLS (best zero-trust, large platform commitment); (c) NLB passthrough (end to end but loses L7 routing, WAF, path rules).
  4. How I'd verify: a load test of re-encryption: bulk TLS adds roughly 1 to 2% CPU with AES-NI; handshakes are the cost and long-lived keepalive connections amortise them. Measure p99 before and after.
  5. Root cause (of the requirement): the plain hop inside the network is the audit finding, not a crypto weakness.
  6. Fix: Pick (a) for the payments services in 6 weeks: ALB target group protocol HTTPS, pods serve certs from a short-lived internal CA (cert-manager), with keepalive on. Roadmap the mesh later for service to service. Cost: about 1 to 2% CPU plus cert operations.
  7. Prevention: Alert on pod certificate expiry; automate rotation; policy check that no target group uses HTTP for the payments namespace.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not passthrough, because it loses WAF and routing we depend on. Not a full mesh in 6 weeks: operationally heavy and a hard-to-undo platform decision. Re-encrypt is reversible.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does the ALB verify pod certs? -> ALB does not validate backend certificates the way a client does (verify); treat it as encryption, and use the mesh for identity.
  • Mesh latency? -> About 1 ms per hop is the usual estimate; measure in your environment.
  • Wildcard cert on all pods? -> Convenient but a single leak exposes everything; prefer per-service short-lived certs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team assumed re-encryption would double CPU. Measuring showed 1.5%, and the real work was certificate rotation. They automated that first and the compliance finding closed in a month.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says TLS inside is too slow.
  • Hire: compares options with cost and capability trade-offs.
  • Strong hire: scopes the requirement, measures, separates reversible from one-way decisions and plans certificate operations.

questions.promptHtml: How do TLS session tickets and 0-RTT work, and why is 0-RTT considered risky?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who know "resumption" from those who understand replay, idempotency and fleet-wide key management.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: After the first handshake the server hands the client an encrypted ticket holding the session state. On reconnect the client sends the ticket, both sides derive keys from a pre-shared key, and the server can skip the certificate and signature, which saves CPU. It still costs 1 RTT. 0-RTT lets the client send the request in the very first flight with zero extra round trip, but that data is replayable, so I allow it only for idempotent requests like GET.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The ticket is encrypted with a server-side ticket key, so the server stores nothing per session. In a fleet, every server must share ticket keys (rotated every 12 to 24 hours, keep the previous key for decrypt) or resumption fails whenever the load balancer picks a different node. Contrast session IDs, which need server-side state.

Full handshake     : ClientHello -> cert + signature -> Finished  (1 RTT, heavy CPU)
Resumed (ticket)   : ClientHello+PSK -> Finished                  (1 RTT, light CPU)
0-RTT (early data) : ClientHello+PSK+HTTP request in same flight  (0 extra RTT, replayable)

Replay: an attacker records the first flight and resends it. The server decrypts it validly. Server-side anti-replay caches help only partly across a fleet. Cloudflare marks such requests with Early-Data: 1 so origins can answer 425 Too Early.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# nginx: forward the signal and share ticket keys across nodes
# ssl_early_data on;
# proxy_set_header Early-Data $ssl_early_data;
# ssl_session_ticket_key /etc/nginx/ticket.current.key;
# ssl_session_ticket_key /etc/nginx/ticket.previous.key;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• 0-RTT on POST /payments.
  • Per-node random ticket keys so resumption fails behind a load balancer.
  • Writing ticket keys to disk or never rotating them (weakens forward secrecy for resumed sessions).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does resumption save a round trip? -> No (still 1 RTT in TLS 1.3 over TCP); it saves CPU and bytes.
  2. How do you make 0-RTT safe? -> Only safe methods, forward Early-Data, reply 425 for others, idempotency keys.
  3. What does a leaked ticket key expose? -> Sessions resumed with tickets under that key become decryptable, so rotate often and keep keys in memory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "faster reconnects". The senior separates CPU savings from latency savings, explains replay, names the 425 mechanism and fleet key sharing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A scale-out from 1 to 6 nodes tripled handshake CPU because ticket keys were per node; sharing one rotating key restored resumption.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the TLS 1.3 handshake. Why is it one round trip, and what is encrypted?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A strong candidate explains the key-share guess and what moved to encrypted records, not just "1.3 is faster".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In TLS 1.3 the client guesses the key exchange group and sends its ECDHE public value in the ClientHello along with SNI and ALPN. The server replies with its own key share, so both compute keys right then. Everything after ServerHello, including the certificate, is already encrypted. The server adds a signature over the transcript and Finished, the client sends Finished and can include the HTTP request in the same flight. One round trip, versus two in TLS 1.2, plus the TCP handshake before it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client                                   Server
 | -- ClientHello (key_share, SNI,ALPN)->|
 | <- ServerHello (key_share)            |   keys derived here
 |    {EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, |
 |     CertificateVerify, Finished} ---- |
 | -- {Finished} + HTTP request -------> |
  • Key share guessing: if the server needs a different group it sends HelloRetryRequest, costing another round trip. X25519 is the safe guess.
  • Certificate is encrypted, so passive observers no longer see which cert is served (SNI still shows the name without ECH).
  • CertificateVerify is a signature over the transcript hash proving the server holds the certificate key.
  • Removed: static RSA key exchange, CBC modes, RC4, compression, renegotiation. All cipher suites give forward secrecy.
  • Total before request with TCP: 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS). QUIC merges them into one.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting two RTT for 1.3 or forgetting the TCP RTT.
  • Thinking the certificate encrypts data; it authenticates the exchange.
  • Not knowing HelloRetryRequest exists.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if client and server share no key-share group? -> HelloRetryRequest adds a round trip.
  2. What is ALPN for? -> Negotiates h2 or h3 during the handshake without extra RTT.
  3. Why is the handshake harder to downgrade? -> The transcript is signed and Finished covers it; 1.3 also embeds a downgrade sentinel in the server random.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "1.3 is one RTT". The senior explains why (key share in the first flight), what is encrypted, what can add a round trip, and what was removed for safety.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An old middlebox that mangled unknown extensions forced a client fleet back to TLS 1.2 until the box was updated, visible as a jump in handshake latency by protocol version.

questions.contextHtml:
A mobile API on nginx was scaled from 1 node to 6 behind an L4 NLB to handle a campaign. CPU on the TLS tier went from 35% to 78% with traffic only 2x higher. Metrics:

              before(1 node)   after(6 nodes)
req/s            3,000            6,000
full hs/s          300            1,850
resumed hs/s     2,700              350
node CPU           35%              78%

The new nodes are a smaller instance type. A dev says the NLB must be dropping packets.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale out more nodes" or blames the instance type. That makes handshake CPU worse in absolute terms.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the resume rate vary by node? Are ticket keys configured explicitly or auto-generated per process? Did cert key type change? Are clients reconnecting more (idle timeout shorter)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower CPU pressure right away: raise the node count temporarily or shed non-critical traffic, but the real fix is next.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-node ticket keys, so a ticket from node A fails on node B, (b) session cache not shared, (c) ticket lifetime shortened, (d) instance type slower.
  4. How I'd verify each: compare $ssl_session_reused logged per node; reuse should be 90% (2,700/3,000) not 6% (350/6,000). Resume rate near 1/6 of the old rate matches random node choice. Check ssl_session_ticket_key presence in config.
  5. Root cause: With 6 nodes and random flow hashing, only about 1 in 6 reconnects land on the node that issued the ticket. Full handshakes with signatures went up 6x.
  6. Fix: Short term: distribute one shared ticket key file to all nodes with rotation (new key first, old key still accepted). Long term: manage keys through a secrets system and rotate automatically every 12 to 24 hours. Consider ECDSA certificates to cut full handshake cost.
  7. Prevention: Dashboard of resumption ratio; alert when it drops below baseline after any scale event; load test with multiple nodes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not disable tickets (more CPU). I would not store keys on disk long term. Sharing keys widens the blast radius of a leak, so rotate often.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not sticky routing at the NLB? -> It couples TLS to affinity and fails when a node dies; shared keys are simpler.
  • CPU still high after fix? -> Check for RSA certs; ECDSA signs about 20x faster.
  • Does resumption need clients to cooperate? -> Yes; if a client does not store tickets (some libraries), it always does full handshakes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a scale-out the team added hardware for weeks. A single config line of shared ticket keys dropped CPU by 40% and cut mobile reconnect time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds servers or blames network.
  • Hire: spots per-node ticket keys with metric evidence.
  • Strong hire: shares and rotates keys safely, adds resumption-ratio alerting, mentions ECDSA.

questions.contextHtml: Saturday 00:00 UTC, the public API returned handshake failures for 3 hours 40 minutes (error rate 100%, servers healthy, CPU 4%). The cert was issued by an ACME client on a single bastion VM with a cron job. A firewall change two months ago blocked port 80 so renewals silently failed. Monitoring: the internal uptime check calls https://localhost/health with curl -k. On-call needed 90 minutes to find the cause because the dashboards were green.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the post-incident review: what failed and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Be more careful about renewals" or a calendar reminder. It treats it as human error instead of a missing system.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many certs exist and where (inventory)? Who owned renewal? What does the ACME log say? Do other certs (internal, partner mTLS, intermediates) have the same risk?
  2. Immediate mitigation (what the response should have been): Renew manually or issue a new cert and reload; the first check on 100% handshake errors with healthy servers is openssl s_client and the notAfter date.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what stalled diagnosis): dashboards watched servers, not the client-visible handshake.
  4. How I'd verify the gaps: echo | openssl s_client -connect api:443 | openssl x509 -noout -enddate; renewal logs; inventory of all certs by expiry.
  5. Root cause: Chain of failures: renewal depended on a single VM and open port 80 (HTTP-01), the failure was silent, monitoring used -k so it could not see expiry, and nobody was alerted at 30/14/7 days.
  6. Fix: Short term: renew and reload. Long term: managed certificates (ACM) or ACME with DNS-01 and a HA renewer, an inventory, and removal of -k.
  7. Prevention: External probe with full verification every minute; alert at 30, 14, 7, 3 days on days-to-expiry from the outside; renewal job success metric; the same for intermediates, internal CAs and mTLS certs; a runbook starting with "check cert dates".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not shorten certificate life without automation first. I would not accept a calendar reminder as the control. Managed certs trade key export for fewer incidents.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Shorter lifetimes are coming; impact? -> More renewals; manual processes will break. Confirm current CA/Browser Forum limits (verify).
  • A partner pins our certificate; renewal breaks them? -> Coordinate or give them the SPKI of a stable key; reuse the key on renewal if allowed.
  • Where does the CA root expiry fit? -> Track trust-store events like a root expiring; they hit old devices.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A large service went dark because an intermediate expired, not the leaf. The inventory only listed leaves. Afterwards every cert in the chain was monitored.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames individual.
  • Hire: finds silent renewal failure and the -k blind spot, adds expiry alerts.
  • Strong hire: full inventory, external verified probes, managed or HA issuance, chain and partner certs covered.

questions.contextHtml: Your Android and iOS apps hard-pin the SPKI hash of the server's leaf key. 2.4 million monthly users; 18% are on app versions older than 12 months and release adoption takes about 6 months to reach 95%. Security wants to rotate the server key (after an employee departure) in 3 weeks. Last year a similar rotation broke 9% of the user base for two days. The pin set contains only the one current key. There is no remote kill switch.
questions.promptHtml: How do you rotate the key without an outage, and what do you change structurally?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Ship a new app and rotate once everyone updates" (cannot wait), or "just rotate and force-update".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the rotation driven by compromise (must be fast) or hygiene? Do the apps pin the leaf, intermediate or a CA? Do old versions support more than one pin? Can the old key be kept alive for the transition?
  2. Immediate mitigation: If the old key may be compromised, treat as a security incident. If hygiene, I can wait: rotating is not urgent enough to break 18% of users.
  3. Hypotheses (options) ranked: (a) keep the old key on the server until old app versions age out, adding a backup pin in new releases; (b) rotate the leaf but pin to a stable intermediate SPKI; (c) force-update gate; (d) remove pinning and rely on Certificate Transparency.
  4. How I'd verify: Handshake failure rate by app version in a canary; Android network_security_config pin-set with an expiration and a backup pin; test an old build against a staging endpoint with the new chain.
  5. Root cause of the fragility: a single pin, no backup, no remote config, pinning the leaf.
  6. Fix: Short term: do not rotate until adoption of a release that carries a backup pin (the new key's SPKI, pre-generated and held offline) passes about 95%; renew certificates with the same key pair meanwhile if policy allows (reuse key; verify the ACME client option). Long term: pin an intermediate plus a backup, set pin expiry, and add a server-side config to relax pinning.
  7. Prevention: Per-version handshake failure alert; runbook for pin rotation with a 12-month horizon; keep backup key in a vault.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not do a big-bang rotation. Pinning an intermediate trades some CA-compromise protection for operability. Hard pinning is a one-way door on mobile; I would weigh dropping it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• If the key is compromised and we must rotate now? -> Do a staged canary, accept breaking old versions, communicate, and push a force-update for old builds.
  • How do you test? -> Old app builds against a staging host with the new cert in CI.
  • Can users be forced to update? -> Yes via an in-app minimum-version gate, at a product cost.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team rotated at renewal because "the CA required it" and lost 9% of sessions for two days. The next time they had a backup pin four releases earlier and rotation was invisible.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rotates and forces updates.
  • Hire: backup pins and staged rollout.
  • Strong hire: ties rotation to adoption data, pins intermediate, pin expiry, failure-by-version alerts, and questions the pin's value.

questions.contextHtml: A push notification campaign and a load balancer restart cause 2 million phone clients to reconnect within 60 seconds. The TLS tier is 16-core nodes; each core can do about 1,000 RSA-2048 full handshakes/s (about 1 ms) or about 20,000 ECDSA P-256 handshakes/s (about 0.05 ms). You have 4 nodes. Last time the TLS tier hit 100% CPU and p99 went from 80 ms to 9 s. Cert is RSA-2048. Resumption rate in steady state is about 60%.
questions.promptHtml: Size it, then tell me what you change so this never causes an outage.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Autoscale", ignoring that autoscaling reacts in minutes while the storm lasts one.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the storm mostly new clients or resumable ones? Can the client back off? Are connections long-lived (WebSocket) or short? Which part hit CPU: handshakes or bulk data?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load gracefully (connection rate limit at the edge), prefer resumed connections, temporarily scale up.
  3. Hypotheses (sizing math): 2,000,000 / 60 s = 33,333 handshakes/s. With 40% not resumable that is about 13,300 full handshakes/s; RSA at 1 ms = 13.3 cores busy, 4 nodes x 16 = 64 cores so 21%... but if the resume rate drops to 0 after restart (ticket keys regenerated at restart), all 33,333 are full: 33 cores, about half the tier, before the 9 s p99 cause (queueing at the accept loop). Compare ECDSA: 33,333 x 0.05 ms = 1.7 cores.
  4. How I'd verify: log full vs resumed handshakes; check whether ticket keys survive a restart; per-core CPU in perf top (bignum modexp for RSA); compare accept queue drops (ss -lnt Recv-Q).
  5. Root cause: restart wiped ticket keys, so everyone did full RSA handshakes at once, plus synchronized reconnects with no jitter.
  6. Fix: Short term: share and persist ticket keys across restarts (in memory distribution, not disk), roll restarts one node at a time with connection draining. Long term: ECDSA certificates (about 20x cheaper), client-side exponential backoff with jitter, rate-limit new handshakes, and terminate at an edge with more headroom.
  7. Prevention: Load-test a 2M reconnect scenario; alert on full-handshake rate; avoid restarting all nodes together.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just add RSA hardware. Dual RSA and ECDSA certs preserve old-client support (reversible). Rate limiting delays some users but protects everyone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did p99 reach 9 s at 50% CPU? -> Queueing and accept-queue overflow in a burst, not average CPU.
  • Can I use a TLS accelerator? -> Possible, but ECDSA and resumption remove the need.
  • What about mobile clients behind carrier NAT? -> No impact on TLS cost, but source-IP rate limits would hit many users together.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A restart at lunchtime made every phone reconnect at once. Moving to ECDSA and adding jitter in the client made the next restart a non-event.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says "autoscale".
  • Hire: does the handshake math, identifies RSA and resumption loss.
  • Strong hire: ECDSA, shared persistent-in-memory ticket keys, jittered backoff, rolling restarts and test plan.
